title: Navigation for a small clinic
metaTitle: Small clinic website navigation in patient words
excerpt: Clinic navigation should use the words patients already say, and keep one path that books a visit. A list of departments makes an anxious person translate before they can act.
alt: Three hands holding coffee cups together over a wooden table, two with latte art, a small group gathered around one surface for a navigation scheme that should gather the real jobs in one place.
caption: Three cups over one table. The menu should gather the real choices, not invent more. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What links belong in a clinic header?
faqs.answer: The visits, the clinician, the fee, how to arrive, and a way to book. Use patient words. Put policies, staff hobbies, and old news in the footer if you keep them at all. The header is for someone who is deciding whether they can come in.

faqs.question: Should Book a visit be visible on a phone?
faqs.answer: Yes. The booking, or the phone number, should be on screen without a hunt, and a menu icon can hold the other jobs. It should not be the only way to start a visit. Anxious patients often give the page one look, so the action has to be in that look.

faqs.question: How do we label clinical services in the menu?
faqs.answer: Label the visit the patient would ask for, not the internal department. "First visit" beats "Patient services." If you need the clinical term, put it on the page, not as the only words in the menu. People in pain will not decode a brand name for a appointment type.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results
How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Small clinic website navigation is a map of jobs, not a list of departments. A patient who is already anxious should see words they would use on the phone, and one path that books a visit.

If the header says "Departments," "Patient resources," and "About our philosophy," they have to translate before they can move. Translation is a poor use of the little attention they brought.

## The jobs, in the order of a worried visit

A first-time patient is trying to do a short list. Understand the visit. See the person and the room. Check the fee and the location. Book or call. The header should be that list, in language from your last twenty phone calls, not from an org chart.

Google's guidance on title links favors titles that are descriptive and concise. Navigation labels are the titles people see first. "Resources" is not descriptive. "How to prepare" is, if a preparation page exists. "Services" is weak if it opens a procedure catalog. "Visits" or "First visit" is closer to the job. The label and the page title should agree, so the patient who taps is not surprised by a different subject.

Nielsen Norman Group found that people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that they read only about a quarter of the text on pages they do open. A menu cannot depend on a paragraph inside the dropdown. If you need a paragraph, the label is wrong or the page is doing too many jobs. Fix the words until a tap is enough.

Cover the logo and read the header to someone who has never been to the clinic. Ask where they would tap to book, to find the fee, and to see who they will meet. Wrong answers are your next draft. Do not explain the logic to them first. The header will not be there to explain itself on a Tuesday night.

## Words from the phone, not from the software

Export the appointment names from the diary and set them beside a list of phrases patients actually say. Where they differ, the patient phrase wins in the nav. The software name can remain inside the diary. Patients should not have to learn it.

Keep one name across the homepage, the menu, the fee, and the booking widget. If the button says "Book a first visit," the menu should not say "Initial assessment" unless you explain they are the same thing in four words. Synonyms feel tidy in a spreadsheet. They feel like a wrong door to a person who is afraid of booking the wrong door.

Avoid cute labels. "Your journey" is not a place. "The team" is acceptable if the page is the people they will meet. "Our story" is acceptable only if that page is short and the people are at the top. When in doubt, use the noun. Visits. Fees. Find us. Book.

Clinical abbreviations belong on the page for referrers, not as the only menu item. A referrer and a frightened patient may share a site, but they should not be forced through the same label. If referrers are a real audience, give them a clearly named link, "For referrers," and keep the patient path in patient words. Two audiences in one unlabeled menu produce a menu nobody trusts.

## One path that books

One item is the action. Book a visit. Style it as the action. On a phone, keep it visible beside the wordmark. The rest can sit in a short menu. A patient should not have to open the menu to do the thing they came to do.

The phone number can sit with the action if many of your bookings are calls. Make it a tap-to-call link with the number visible as text. An icon of a phone with no number is a puzzle. Hours can be in the menu item "Find us," not crammed into the bar until the booking wraps onto two lines.

Do not add "Patient portal" at the same visual weight as booking unless most visitors are existing patients logging in. New patients will tap it and feel stupid when it asks for credentials they do not have. Put the portal in the footer or behind a quiet "Existing patients" label. Protect the new-patient path from looking like a login wall.

If a chat tool covers the booking on a small screen, move the tool. The nav's job is lost the moment another layer eats the button. Anxious people do not enjoy dismissing popovers before they are allowed to book.

## What stays in the header

A small clinic header can be five items and a button.

- Visits, in patient language.
- The clinician or the team.
- Fees.
- Find us: address, hours, access.
- Book a visit.
- A visible phone number if calls are how you work.

That is a complete marketing site for many clinics. News, a blog, and a gallery are optional and should earn their place with a current habit of publishing. An empty "Blog" link is a promise you are behind. Remove it until you are not.

Dropdowns make sense when the visit types are truly different and a patient must choose. They do not make sense as a parking lot for PDFs. Preparation sheets can live on the visit page they belong to. A menu of twelve documents is how people miss the booking.

Order the items as a first visit would need them. Do not lead with "About." Lead with the visit or with the booking, then the facts that unblock the booking. Philosophy is last if it is present at all.

## What stays in the footer

The footer is for deliberate looking. Privacy, records requests, the registration numbers, a postal address, cancellations, and the existing-patient portal. Label cancellations as cancellations. A patient who needs to cancel is often embarrassed. Do not make them hunt through "Contact" to undo a visit.

Repeat the main jobs in the same words as the header. The footer is the recovery path when the header was too clever or the thumb missed. Do not introduce "Our modalities" at the bottom if the header said "Visits."

Include the access fact in "Find us," and repeat it in the footer if the page is long. Stairs, elevator, step-free route. Patients who need that fact are not helped by a decorative map with no words. Write the sentence. Link to the map second.

Skip a column of keyword pages. A clinic does not need ten near-duplicate location pages to be found by the neighborhood it is actually in. One honest location page, with the real instructions, beats a net of thin ones. Google's title guidance is a reminder that each linked page should be a real subject. A doorway to an empty subject is clutter.

## The phone menu is the menu

Design the collapsed header before the wide one. Wordmark, booking, phone. Then a list that repeats the four jobs in the same order. Large tap targets. No autoplay. No promotional card inside the menu. The person opened it to go somewhere.

When they choose, close the menu and move focus to the heading of the new page. A menu that stays open over the fee table is a trap. Test with a thumb, not with a mouse on a stretched browser. The cursor is more precise than the person you are designing for.

Check the booking widget itself. If it has its own navigation, its labels must match. A widget that says "Select a department" after a header that said "First visit" has restarted the anxiety. Pass the visit type in. Ask only what the widget truly needs. The menu's promise dies inside a widget that contradicts it.

Hanabi designs and builds the header as part of the site, not as a theme option filled in later. If you want that structure looked at against your diary, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the appointment names and the phrases patients use. The call should end with a shorter list of labels.

## An hour to rename the map

Write the current header in a column. For each item, write the patient phrase it is supposed to be. If you cannot, the item is a candidate to merge or cut. Then click every item on a phone and write down the page title that appears. Disagreements are bugs.

Call the desk and ask them to book using only the words in the new header. If they stumble, the header is still internal. Change it until the call sounds like the menu, and the menu sounds like the call.

Revisit the labels when you add a visit type. New services often arrive as a new menu item before anyone asks whether they are a boundary on an existing visit. Growth of the menu is not growth of the clinic. A stable, small map is a form of care.

Pictures are the next labels patients read, and they can undo a clear menu in one stock smile. [Photography direction for a small clinic](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-small-clinic) is about showing the room and the clinician, and refusing the pictures that only look like care.
